item.title: Deep dive: Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) in adult ICU
item.description:
Secondary HLH in adults is a sepsis mimic that is easily missed. The episode covers when to suspect it (the three Fs of fever, falling counts and raised ferritin, with organ failure not responding to treatment), the HScore against the HLH-2004 criteria and their limits in critical care, the main triggers (infection including EBV, lymphoma, autoimmune disease or macrophage activation syndrome, and CAR T related IEC-HS), and the largely observational evidence for dexamethasone, etoposide, anakinra, emapalumab and ruxolitinib. It reports ICU mortality of 57 percent in a large French cohort, and stresses early haematology involvement. Reference points are the 2023 UK HiHASC guideline and the Histiocyte Society adult recommendations.

Take-home points

  • Fever, falling counts and raised ferritin in a patient not responding as expected: check triglycerides, fibrinogen, liver tests and film, and calculate the HScore.
  • Call haematology the day you think of it, and agree dexamethasone, anakinra and whether etoposide is needed.
  • Hunt the trigger hard: lymphoma, EBV and other viral PCRs, autoimmune disease, recent CAR T.
  • Be honest with families: ICU mortality was over half in the largest cohort and the drug evidence is observational.

item.title: Deep dive: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura on ICU
item.description:
Immune TTP from the ICU perspective: suspect it early from thrombocytopenia plus microangiopathic haemolysis with a normal coagulation screen, send ADAMTS13 before any plasma (the PLASMIC score is a bridge, and BSH prefers early ADAMTS13 to scores), and start plasma exchange within four to eight hours with steroids, then rituximab and caplacizumab. HERCULES and large real-world and retrospective cohorts support caplacizumab, at the cost of more mucocutaneous bleeding; the single-arm MAYARI trial (registry results) shows exchange-free treatment works in milder, French score 1 or 2 patients but does not apply to critically ill presentations. Troponin, age and neurological involvement mark high risk, platelet transfusion is avoided except for life-threatening bleeding, recombinant ADAMTS13 is now preferred for congenital TTP prophylaxis, and relapse surveillance with ADAMTS13 and pre-emptive rituximab matters because survivors carry excess stroke and other long-term morbidity.

Take-home points

  • Suspect TTP early and send ADAMTS13 activity and antibody before any plasma, but do not wait for the result.
  • Call the TTP centre and start plasma exchange within hours with steroids, then rituximab and caplacizumab once TTP is confirmed.
  • Avoid platelet transfusion unless there is life-threatening bleeding, and check troponin and ECG in everyone.
  • Monitor ADAMTS13 after discharge; pre-emptive rituximab below 20 IU/dL prevents relapse.

item.title: Deep dive: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome on ICU
item.description:
Adult HUS as it presents to ICU. Sort immune TTP, STEC-HUS, complement-mediated (atypical) HUS and secondary TMAs on day one: ADAMTS13 activity, stool Shiga toxin PCR and complement studies before plasma, and early phone contact with the National aHUS Service in Newcastle (NHS England funding via Blueteq). Plasma exchange is a bridge until TTP is excluded. STEC-HUS evidence (2012 German outbreak case-control study; ECULISHU in children) does not support eculizumab. For aHUS, eculizumab and ravulizumab evidence is from single-arm trials; the UK SETS aHUS trial suggests selected patients can stop with monitoring. Meningococcal vaccination (MenACWY and Bexsero), antibiotic prophylaxis and renal outcomes are covered.

Take-home points

  • Before plasma: ADAMTS13 activity, stool Shiga toxin PCR and complement bloods.
  • Ring the National aHUS Service in Newcastle early; funding goes through Blueteq.
  • Plasma exchange is a bridge until TTP is excluded, not a treatment for aHUS.
  • STEC-HUS is managed supportively; eculizumab is not funded there and the trials are negative on the acute endpoint.
  • If aHUS: vaccinate (MenACWY and Bexsero) and give antibiotic prophylaxis, and plan for individualised withdrawal rather than assuming lifelong therapy.

item.title: Deep dive: Delirium and sedation on ICU
item.description:
A consultant-level review of ICU sedation and delirium trials. For antipsychotics, MIND-USA (NEJM 2018) and AID-ICU (NEJM 2022) found that haloperidol does not shorten delirium or increase days alive out of hospital. AID-ICU's secondary outcome of mortality was lower with haloperidol at 90 days (36.3 vs 43.3 percent) and at one year, which is a signal, not proof. Prophylactic haloperidol (REDUCE) did not help. For dexmedetomidine, SPICE III showed no overall mortality difference, but a post hoc Bayesian analysis suggested benefit over 65 and harm at 65 or under, which led to a 2022 safety letter agreed with the MHRA. MENDS2 found no difference from propofol in sepsis, and the UK A2B trial (JAMA 2025) found no faster extubation with dexmedetomidine or clonidine compared with propofol, with more agitation and bradycardia. NONSEDA found no advantage for no sedation over light sedation. Pro-MEDIC and the meta-analysis restricted to low risk-of-bias trials found no delirium benefit from melatonin. ABCDEF evidence is mostly observational. R2D2-ICU (JAMA 2026) found that avoiding routine wrist restraints did not increase self-extubation. BRAIN-ICU links longer delirium to lasting cognitive impairment. The 2025 PADIS focused update suggests dexmedetomidine over propofol and suggests melatonin, but it was published before A2B. UK guidance (NICE CG103 and GPICS V3, 2026) does not name a sedative, and UK practice remains propofol first. SESAR (JAMA 2025) found worse survival with sevoflurane than with propofol in ARDS.

Take-home points

  • Aim for light sedation with a daily look at a sedation hold; NONSEDA doesn't justify deeper sedation or no sedation.
  • Propofol remains a reasonable first-line sedative: A2B found no faster extubation with dexmedetomidine or clonidine, and more agitation and bradycardia.
  • If using dexmedetomidine, consider age: the SPICE III signal and the 2022 safety letter point to caution in patients 65 or younger.
  • Haloperidol doesn't shorten delirium and shouldn't be used as prophylaxis; short courses for distress are reasonable, and AID-ICU is reassuring on safety.
  • Melatonin is cheap and probably harmless, but the best trials show no delirium benefit; put effort into the bundle (mobilisation, sleep, family, fewer restraints).

item.title: Deep dive: Post-intensive care syndrome and recovery after ICU
item.description:
A consultant-level review of what has been tested for recovery after critical illness. Nurse-led follow-up clinics (PRaCTICaL, BMJ 2009) and primary-care case management (SMOOTH, JAMA 2016) did not improve quality of life, and the 2018 Cochrane review found little or no effect. InS:PIRE (Thorax 2023) was positive but non-randomised. For in-ICU mobilisation, Schweickert (Lancet 2009) improved functional independence, but EPICC (Thorax 2018) and TEAM (NEJM 2022) were neutral, and TEAM showed more mobilisation-related adverse events (9.2% vs 4.1%) and a non-significant excess of deaths. Meta-analyses (Paton, Lancet Respir Med 2024; Crit Care Med 2025) found no mortality effect and less ICU-acquired weakness, and the SCCM PADIS 2025 focused update conditionally recommends enhanced mobilisation. CYCLE (NEJM Evid 2024) was neutral. On diaries, the positive RACHEL trial (2010) was followed by a neutral French trial (JAMA 2019), and a September 2026 meta-analysis found no PTSD effect after correcting for publication bias. Post-discharge rehabilitation trials have been neutral: Elliott 2011, RECOVER 2015 and the UK iRehab trial (JAMA, July 2026). A Brazilian stepped-wedge telehealth trial (JAMA, September 2026) improved quality of life overall but not among survivors, and the authors suggest lower mortality may explain this. Family interventions have either backfired (Carson, JAMA 2016) or been neutral (FICUS, ICM 2026). NICE CG83 (2009, reviewed 2018 with no update) asks for a reassessment at 2 to 3 months. GPICS V3 (January 2026) now makes a post-ICU recovery clinic a minimum standard, which is ahead of the trial evidence. NCEPOD's Recovery Beyond Survival (June 2025) found poor delivery. Five-year mortality among hospital survivors in Scotland was 32% vs 23% in matched controls, and only about 55% of survivors were back at work at 12 months.

Take-home points

  • Keep mobilising, but don't chase intensity: TEAM showed no benefit from more and more adverse events.
  • Follow-up clinics are now a GPICS V3 minimum standard, though no trial shows they improve quality of life. Run yours as needs-finding and audit what you find.
  • ICU diaries are cheap and humane but don't reliably prevent PTSD.
  • Families can be harmed by well-meant interventions. Watch for distress rather than assuming support helps.
  • Ask about work, money and family at follow-up, because that's where the long-term burden falls.

item.title: Deep dive: Organ donation after circulatory death
item.description:
DCD now makes up most UK deceased donation (792 of 1,428 deceased donors in 2025/26, NHSBT), while consent/authorisation fell to 57% overall and about 53% for DCD. Law: Wales (own Act, deemed consent from 1 Dec 2015), England (Organ Donation (Deemed Consent) Act 2019 amending HTA 2004 s3(6)(ba)/(6A)/(6B), from 20 May 2020), Scotland (Human Tissue (Authorisation) (Scotland) Act 2019, deemed authorisation from 26 Mar 2021) and Northern Ireland (2022 Act inserting HTA s3(6AA)/(9A); deemed consent in effect from 1 June 2023). In England consent is deemed unless a person in a qualifying relationship provides information that would lead a reasonable person to conclude the person would not have consented; HTA Code F says relatives have no legal right to revoke a valid decision but donation need not proceed where public confidence is at risk. Excepted adults include those who lacked capacity to understand deemed consent for a significant period before death (HTA guidance: 12 months), which captures many PDOC patients. Pre-mortem steps in England/Wales rest on MCA best interests per DH 2009 guidance (heparin, resuscitation, femoral cannulation unlikely ever to be in best interests; seek Court of Protection declaration); the 2021 UK NRP protocol says no pre-mortem interventions are currently allowed in controlled DCD. Scotland alone has a statutory pre-death procedures regime (Type A: SSI 2020/80; Type B incl. CT, MRI, bronchoscopy, needing two doctors independent of retrieval: SSI 2021/110); heparin is on neither list. The 2025 AoMRC Code leaves the five-minute observation unchanged (circulatory criteria not in its list of major changes) but specifies ventilator disconnection before the five minutes, start at mechanical asystole (arterial line or echo acceptable; ECG asystole not required), corneal reflexes recommended soon after arrest, independence from retrieval, and that post-mortem perfusion protocols must ensure no blood circulation to the brain. Dhanani NEJM 2021 (631 patients) found transient cardiac activity after pulselessness in 14% on waveform review, all within 4 min 20 s; a 2023 systematic review rated five minutes sufficient for controlled DCD (moderate certainty). A-NRP is being rolled out nationally by 2027 with NICE guidance due Nov 2026; TA-NRP remains contested (ACP 2021 call for a pause; UK-Canadian permanence proposal; retrospective data showing less severe PGD). Uncontrolled DCD is a Cambridge pilot only. The RCP 2020 PDOC guideline states donation is not possible after CANH withdrawal. Of 1,037 consented DCD patients in 2025/26, 266 did not donate, 52% of them because of prolonged time to asystole; length of process was the commonest family reason for declining DCD (20%).

Take-home points

  • Make the withdrawal decision first, on its own merits in the patient's best interests, independently of donation, and document it.
  • Under deemed consent the family's role is to give information about the patient's own view; check excepted-adult status (lack of capacity for a significant period, HTA guidance 12 months), which often applies in PDOC.
  • Pre-mortem steps must be in the patient's best interests and not cause harm or distress; under the current (2021) national NRP protocol there is no pre-mortem heparin or cannulation in UK controlled DCD, and Scotland has a statutory Type A/Type B list.
  • Confirm death after five full minutes, off the ventilator, observed in person, by a clinician independent of the retrieval team, as the 2025 AoMRC Code sets out.
  • Families most often decline DCD because the process takes too long; plan logistics early and be honest about timescales.

item.title: Deep dive: Assessing capacity on ICU
item.description:
A consultant-level look at the hard capacity cases on ICU. Clinicians tend to overestimate capacity in awake ICU patients (Bertrand 2019: physicians judged 45 percent capable against 17 percent by a structured score, which is not the legal test). The Supreme Court in A Local Authority v JB [2021] UKSC 52 sets the structure: s2(1) is the single test, approached functional question first and then the causative nexus (paras 65-79), with fluctuation as a qualification to the assessment (para 64). For delirium and fluctuating capacity the episode contrasts Hedley's longitudinal approach to repeated decisions (Cheshire West v PWK) with one-off ICU decisions, uses the 2007 Code (paras 3.14, 4.26-4.27) and shows what all practicable steps looked like in Royal Free v RH [2026] EWCOP 17. On refusal: King's College Hospital v C (unwise is not incapacity; choosing to give information no weight is not inability to use or weigh it) versus A NHS Trust v ST (not believing a well-founded prognosis held to be incapacity; contested). Advance decisions: s25 validity and applicability, s25(5)-(6) formalities, Barnsley v MSP (non-compliant document still weighty in best interests) and Re AB [2025] EWCOP 20 (Poole J's lessons on ADRTs, prompt applications, s26(5)). LPAs: s9 registration, s11(7)-(8) and Option A on form LP1H. Court applications: NHS Trust v Y and the January 2020 Vice-President's guidance (an application must be made where life-sustaining treatment is in issue and there is disagreement or the case is finely balanced; out-of-hours applications are exceptional). The 2007 Code remains current; no revised Code has been published.

Take-home points

  • Follow JB's sequence and record it: identify the matter, the relevant information in its factual context, whether P is unable to decide, and only then whether that inability is because of an impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain (JB paras 67-79).
  • With delirium, document the practicable steps (timing, sedation holds, repeat attempts with others present) and, for one-off decisions, wait for a lucid window if you safely can (s1(3), s4(3), Code paras 3.14 and 4.27; Royal Free v RH para 27).
  • An unwise refusal of ventilation, dialysis or blood is not incapacity (King's College Hospital v C paras 30 and 38); not believing a well-founded prognosis was held to be incapacity in ST, but that is contested ground.
  • Get the actual advance decision or LPA document: check s25 validity and applicability, the s25(5)-(6) formalities for life-sustaining treatment, LPA registration and Option A for life-sustaining treatment (s11(8)).
  • If there is doubt or dispute over life-sustaining treatment, apply to the Court of Protection promptly and keep treating meanwhile (s26(5), s6(7); 2020 guidance paras 8-9; Re AB para 53.7).

item.title: Deep dive: Ceilings of care and treatment escalation plans
item.description:
A consultant-level, legally precise review of ceilings of care. Evidence: the Cambridge UFTO before-and-after study (PLoS One 2013) found fewer harms in patients not for CPR (rate difference 12.9 per 1000 patient-days; harms contributing to death 23/71 vs 4/44); a 2025 randomised vignette study showed a DNACPR decision reduced geriatricians' willingness to consider NIV (67.3% vs 83.6%) and ICU (10.9% vs 25.5%); the NIHR ReSPECT evaluation (2022) found ReSPECT in 40 of 186 acute hospitals by late 2019, patient/family involvement recorded on 73% of forms, similar harms with or without a form, and conversations ranging from open to 'informing of a decision already made'; a Leeds analysis of 23,729 ReSPECT plans found DNACPR less often recorded for Asian and Black than White patients. Law: Burke [2005] EWCA Civ 1003 (no obligation to provide treatment not clinically indicated, paras 50 and 55, but para 53 on competent patients wanting ANH); Aintree v James [2013] UKSC 67 (court has no greater power than patient, para 18; question is whether giving treatment is in best interests, para 22; widest-sense welfare and consultation, para 39; patient's own perspective, para 45; advance applications, para 47); N v ACCG [2017] UKSC 22 (choice only between available options, para 35); Tracey [2014] EWCA Civ 822 (Article 8 presumption of patient involvement in DNACPR, paras 53 to 55; common law the same, para 89); Winspear [2015] EWHC 3250 (QB) (s4(7) MCA duty to consult carer, paras 45, 50, 52, 59). The pivotal 2026 development is Townsend v Epsom and St Helier [2026] EWCA Civ 195: no carve-out for 'clinical decisions' in incapacitated adults (para 69); unresolved disagreement about life-sustaining treatment must go to court via the commissioner and the hospital cannot pre-empt it by unilateral withholding or withdrawal (para 72); but the court can never compel treatment clinicians consider clinically inappropriate (paras 68(5), 74). The Supreme Court granted permission on 29 June 2026 with the hearing listed for 12 to 13 January 2027. Royal Free v RH [2026] EWCOP 17 (T3) shows trusts starting treatment pending court resolution after Townsend, and a court-approved, permissive ceiling of care. GMC end-of-life guidance (2010, updated 2022 and 2024) paras 16, 47 to 48, 134, 138, 143; joint BMA/RCUK/RCN CPR guidance (3rd edition, 1st revision 2016) is under review; the MCA Code of Practice has not been revised since 2007. Communication advice separates what medicine can achieve from what the patient would want, and avoids asking families to decide (GSTT v VA [2023] EWCOP 39, para 20).

Take-home points

  • A ceiling of care for an incapacitated patient is a best interests decision under the Mental Capacity Act: after Townsend [2026] EWCA Civ 195 (para 69) there is no carve-out for 'clinical decisions'.
  • Nobody, including the Court of Protection, can compel you to give treatment you consider clinically inappropriate (Burke paras 50 and 55; Aintree para 18; N v ACCG para 35; Townsend paras 68(5) and 74).
  • Consult before you record a DNACPR decision: the patient unless it is likely to cause harm (Tracey paras 53 to 55), and the family or carer of an incapacitated patient unless impracticable (Winspear, s4(7) MCA); record why if you do not.
  • Use a TEP or ReSPECT plan to place DNACPR within a wider plan (it applies only to CPR, GMC para 143), and share second opinions with the family promptly.
  • Unresolved disagreement about life-sustaining treatment should go to court via the commissioning body, early (Townsend para 72; Re Y para 125); watch for the Supreme Court hearing on 12 to 13 January 2027.

item.title: Deep dive: Frailty and the older surgical patient
item.description:
A consultant-level look at frailty in older surgical patients for anaesthetists and intensivists. SNAP-3 (BJA 2025; 7,129 UK patients aged 60 and over, 214 hospitals) found that about one in five were frail, and outcomes worsened from a Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) score of 4 upwards. Frailty, more than multimorbidity, drove length of stay, delirium and mortality. The CFS is quick and about as accurate as a modified Fried index (adjusted odds ratio 2.51 for death or new disability at 90 days in a 702-patient Canadian cohort), but it is a baseline population risk marker, poorly validated in younger people or those with stable single-system disability, and it says nothing about the operation. Prehabilitation trials in frail patients (Carli, JAMA Surg 2020; McIsaac's PREHAB, BJA 2022) were neutral. A supervised in-hospital programme in a non-frail colorectal cohort (PREHAB, JAMA Surg 2023) reduced severe complications (17.1 versus 29.7 percent). A 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis of 186 trials favoured exercise, but with very low certainty. Comprehensive geriatric assessment reduces discharge to a higher level of care (Cochrane 2018, mostly hip fracture). The CPOC/BGS 2021 guideline, still current, sets the UK standard: CFS for everyone over 65, CGA and cognitive assessment at CFS 5 or more, and daily 4AT screening. For delirium, regional versus general anaesthesia made no difference (REGAIN, RAGA). EEG guidance was neutral in ENGAGES, and Balanced found no mortality difference between BIS 50 and 35, yet ESAIC 2024 still weakly suggests EEG monitoring. B-Free (benzodiazepine restriction in cardiac surgery) was neutral. Shared decision-making should follow Montgomery and centre on function and going home. ANZICS registry data (BJA 2025) link frailty to shorter long-term survival after postoperative ICU admission (adjusted hazard ratio 2.33).

Take-home points

  • Document a CFS, but read it as a population risk marker: risk climbs from CFS 4, and the score says nothing about the operation.
  • Prehabilitation is reasonable, but the trials in frail patients are neutral; supervised programmes with good adherence look best.
  • Regional versus general anaesthesia doesn't change delirium. Avoid delirium-provoking drugs and excessive depth, and use multicomponent prevention.
  • Get a geriatrician involved early; the best evidence for comprehensive geriatric assessment is in hip fracture.
  • Before surgery, talk about function and going home, and agree the ceiling of treatment, including ICU.

item.title: Deep dive: Airway management in the critically ill
item.description:
A consultant-level look at the trials that have reshaped peri-intubation care in ICU. INTUBE (JAMA 2021, 2,964 patients, 29 countries) found major adverse peri-intubation events in 45.2% of intubations, mostly cardiovascular instability (42.6%), with cardiac arrest in 3.1%. DEVICE (NEJM 2023) improved first-pass success with videolaryngoscopy (85.1% vs 70.8%) without changing severe complications, though more than 90% of operators were trainees. BOUGIE (JAMA 2021) found no first-pass advantage for bougie over stylet (80.4% vs 83.0%). PREOXI (NEJM 2024) halved peri-intubation hypoxaemia with NIV preoxygenation (9.1% vs 18.5%) without more aspiration, and a 2025 network meta-analysis ranked NIV above HFNO above face mask. In the RSI trial (NEJM, online Dec 2025, 2,365 patients), ketamine did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with etomidate (28.1% vs 29.1%) and caused more cardiovascular collapse (22.1% vs 17.0%), which 2026 network meta-analyses support. PrePARE and PREPARE II found no benefit from a routine 500 mL fluid bolus. Trials of prophylactic vasopressors in ICU have not reported (PREVENTION, NCT05014581, registered as recruiting). The UK critical care guideline is still the 2018 DAS/ICS/FICM/RCoA guideline (BJA, online 2017). DAS published its 2025 guideline for unanticipated difficult intubation in adults, which adds a physiologically difficult airway section and keeps a linear Plan A to D, where the ICU guideline combines Plans B and C. We found no 2025 ICS/DAS critical care update.

Take-home points

  • Use a videolaryngoscope first for ICU intubation: DEVICE showed better first-pass success, mainly with less experienced operators, but no fewer severe complications.
  • A stylet is a reasonable default: BOUGIE found no first-pass advantage for bougie-first.
  • Preoxygenate with NIV: PREOXI halved hypoxaemia without increasing aspiration.
  • Ketamine is not the haemodynamically safer choice: in the RSI trial it caused more cardiovascular collapse than etomidate with no mortality difference. Pick the dose carefully and have a vasopressor ready.
  • Don't give a routine fluid bolus to prevent collapse: PrePARE and PREPARE II were both negative.

item.title: Deep dive: Emergency laparotomy: perioperative care and who needs ICU
item.description:
A consultant-level look at emergency laparotomy for anaesthetists and intensivists. The NELA tenth report (October 2025; April 2023 to April 2024, 23,560 patients) gave 30-day mortality of 8.1 percent, down from 11.7 percent in year 1. Consultant presence for high-risk cases is now high (surgeon 96.4 percent, anaesthetist 92.3 percent), and 77.6 percent of high-risk patients went directly to critical care. Timeliness is still poor: 8.4 percent of RCS-Immediate patients reached theatre within 6 hours, and about 15 percent of patients with suspected sepsis received antibiotics within 1 hour. The rebuilt 13-variable NELA parsimonious score (concordance 0.86) discriminates about as well as P-POSSUM in external cohorts, but calibration varies by setting. In NELA patients at extreme risk (predicted mortality of 50 percent or more), some were still alive at 90 days. EPOCH (Lancet 2019), a stepped-wedge quality improvement trial, was neutral. OPTIMISE II (BMJ 2024, elective surgery) found no benefit from cardiac output-guided therapy and more early arrhythmias. FLO-ELA (3,140 patients, recruitment closed November 2024, primary outcome changed to days alive and out of hospital at 90 days) had not published results as of 8 October 2026. Postoperative geriatric review is strongly associated with lower mortality (observational, likely confounded), but only about a third of eligible patients receive it. The first NoLap report (May 2026) found 80 percent 30-day mortality among patients not operated on, and the ELF2 cohort showed that about a fifth survive to 90 days. RCS 2018 standards ask for an in-person three-consultant assessment above 25 percent predicted mortality and direct critical care admission above 5 percent at the end of surgery. A 2026 Australian cohort found the NELA score predicted death but not the need for ICU therapies. Montgomery and McCulloch frame how not operating should be offered and discussed.

Take-home points

  • NELA 30-day mortality is now 8.1 percent, but time to theatre and time to antibiotics remain the weak links.
  • The NELA score is a population estimate: present it as a range, and treat frailty (CFS 5 or more) and missing risk assessments as high risk.
  • Cardiac output-guided fluid has no supporting trial evidence in emergency laparotomy yet: OPTIMISE II was neutral and FLO-ELA has not reported.
  • Involve a geriatrician early: postoperative geriatric review is the strongest (observational) association with survival, yet only about a third of eligible patients get it.
  • Above 25 percent predicted mortality, make the decision jointly at consultant level, offer not operating as a real option, and tell families that some patients survive without surgery.

item.title: Deep dive: Invasive fungal infection on ICU
item.description:
A consultant-level look at invasive fungal infection on ICU. In EMPIRICUS (JAMA 2016, 260 patients), empirical micafungin for ICU-acquired sepsis with multisite Candida colonisation and multi-organ failure did not improve fungal-infection-free survival at day 28 (68% vs 60.2%, HR 1.35, 95% CI 0.87 to 2.08), although it reduced new proven infection (3% vs 12%). The 2016 Cochrane review found no mortality benefit from untargeted antifungals (RR 0.93). In CandiSep (ICM 2022, 339 patients), starting antifungals on a beta-D-glucan of 80 pg/mL or more got treatment in faster but did not reduce 28-day mortality (33.7% vs 30.5%). FUNDICU 2024 left BDG out of its research definition of probable deep-seated candidiasis. Two small single-centre trials (Rouzé 2017, De Pascale 2020) suggest that stopping on a negative biomarker safely shortens empirical therapy. Echinocandins remain first line. In ReSTORE (Lancet 2023), weekly rezafungin was non-inferior to caspofungin; the MHRA approved it in January 2024. Influenza-associated aspergillosis affected 19% of patients with severe influenza on ICU (Schauwvlieghe 2018) and is linked to high mortality. CAPA affected about 15% of ICU COVID patients in the ECMM study. POSA-FLU's prophylaxis trial was inconclusive. Diagnosis rests on lavage galactomannan (index of 1.0 or more), because serum galactomannan is insensitive in non-neutropenic patients. Treatment is voriconazole or isavuconazole, per ESCMID-ECMM-ERS 2017, IDSA 2016, the CAPA consensus and the Swiss FUNGINOS and German AWMF ICU guidelines of 2025. UKHSA's 2025 Candidozyma auris guidance covers admission screening, isolation and contact de-isolation, and says not to treat colonisation and to use an echinocandin first line; C. auris has been notifiable in England since 6 April 2025. Candidaemia is treated for 14 days after clearance, with step-down to an oral azole after 5 to 7 days (IDSA 2016) or at least 5 days (global ECMM/ISHAM/ASM guideline 2025) in stable patients.

Take-home points

  • Don't start empirical echinocandins for colonisation and sepsis alone: EMPIRICUS and CandiSep showed no survival benefit. Treat septic shock with a real Candida risk, and reassess by day 4 to 5.
  • Use beta-D-glucan to stop antifungals rather than to start them: a negative result supports stopping, but a positive one is non-specific.
  • In severe influenza and COVID, look for aspergillus early with lavage galactomannan (serum is insensitive), and treat with voriconazole or isavuconazole.
  • Candida (Candidozyma) auris has been notifiable in England since April 2025. Screen patients admitted after healthcare abroad, isolate or cohort them, and don't treat colonisation. Use an echinocandin for infection.
  • For candidaemia, remove the line early, treat for 14 days from clearance, and step down to fluconazole after about 5 days in stable patients with susceptible isolates and negative repeat cultures.

item.title: Deep dive: Antimicrobial stewardship on ICU
item.description:
A consultant-level look at the stewardship decisions that now have trial evidence. Procalcitonin-guided stopping (PRORATA, SAPS, and the UK ADAPT-Sepsis trial, JAMA 2025) safely shortens courses, but only by about a day, and CRP-guided stopping showed no benefit. Shorter fixed courses are supported by BALANCE (NEJM 2025: 7 vs 14 days for bloodstream infection, excluding S. aureus and severe immunosuppression) and, for VAP, by Chastre (2003) and REGARD-VAP (2024), with residual uncertainty for non-fermenting Gram-negatives and Pseudomonas. BLING III (JAMA 2024) narrowly missed its mortality endpoint for continuous beta-lactam infusion, but the accompanying meta-analysis favoured prolonged infusion, and the Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 guideline now recommends it strongly after a loading dose. Beta-lactam TDM (TARGET, DOLPHIN) improves target attainment but has not improved outcomes. The only de-escalation RCT (Leone 2014) was small and unfavourable. The UK INHALE trial of a multiplex PCR pneumonia panel improved early prescribing but failed to show non-inferior clinical cure. On guidance: NICE NG253 (Nov 2025) has a procalcitonin update in progress, UKHSA's Start Smart Then Focus (2023) sets the 48-72 hour CARES review, an ESICM-endorsed 2020 position paper supports routine beta-lactam TDM, and SSC 2026 makes conditional recommendations for procalcitonin-guided stopping, shorter courses, TDM and rapid diagnostics.

Take-home points

  • For uncomplicated Gram-negative bacteraemia with source control, seven days is the default; BALANCE supports it (it excluded S. aureus and severe immunosuppression).
  • Procalcitonin-guided stopping is safe but saves only about a day (ADAPT-Sepsis); CRP-guided stopping has no trial support.
  • Give piperacillin-tazobactam and meropenem as prolonged or continuous infusions, always after a loading dose (BLING III, the 2024 meta-analysis, SSC 2026 strong recommendation).
  • For VAP, stop once the patient has been stable for 48 hours, often by day seven or earlier (REGARD-VAP); take more care with non-fermenting Gram-negatives.
  • Beta-lactam TDM and rapid multiplex PCR improve process measures but have not yet improved outcomes (TARGET, DOLPHIN, INHALE); use them case by case.

item.title: Deep dive: Nutrition in critical illness
item.description:
A consultant-level look at what recent trials have changed in ICU nutrition. On calories, EDEN (JAMA 2012), PermiT (NEJM 2015) and NUTRIREA-3 (Lancet Respir Med 2023) all found that feeding less in the first week did not increase mortality. In NUTRIREA-3, a low-dose arm (6 kcal/kg/day, 0.2-0.4 g/kg protein) in ventilated patients with shock reached readiness for ICU discharge sooner and had fewer gut and liver complications, and a 2026 post hoc analysis found no excess kidney injury. EPaNIC (NEJM 2011) favoured delaying supplemental PN to day 8. CALORIES and NUTRIREA-2 found no mortality difference by route. On protein, EFFORT Protein (Lancet 2023), PRECISe (Lancet 2024, worse quality of life with 2.0 vs 1.3 g/kg/day) and TARGET Protein (JAMA 2025, no benefit across 3397 patients) were all neutral or harmful. A 2026 meta-analysis (Summers, Clin Nutr) found no mortality effect overall and higher mortality with more protein in AKI (RR 1.29, 3 trials). REPLENISH has not yet reported. ESPEN 2023 is closest to the trials: no more than 70% of energy expenditure early, 80-100% of measured expenditure after day 3, protein 1.3 g/kg/day built up progressively, indirect calorimetry in ventilated patients, and supplemental PN case by case. ASPEN 2022 (12-25 kcal/kg, protein 1.2-2.0 g/kg, no supplemental PN before day 7) predates the protein trials, so its upper protein range now looks too high. NICE CG32 (2006, updated 2017) is not ICU-specific but still supplies the UK refeeding-risk criteria. Doig's 2015 refeeding trial was negative on its primary outcome but found better 60-day survival with 48 hours of caloric restriction (a secondary outcome), and ESPEN has adopted that approach. After ICU, ward intake falls short. INTENT (phase II) increased energy delivery but was not powered for clinical outcomes.

Take-home points

  • Less is fine early: first-week underfeeding caused no harm in EDEN, PermiT or NUTRIREA-3, and in shock it meant fewer gut complications.
  • High protein has not helped and may harm, especially in AKI (EFFORT Protein, PRECISe, TARGET Protein, Summers 2026 meta-analysis). Aim for about 1.3 g/kg/day.
  • Don't start supplemental parenteral nutrition in week one in a previously well-nourished patient (EPaNIC; ASPEN 2022).
  • Check phosphate daily in the first week. If refeeding hypophosphataemia develops, restrict calories for 48 hours and then build back up (Doig 2015; ESPEN 2023).
  • Make sure nutrition carries on after ICU, and don't let the feeding tube come out before the patient is actually eating.

item.title: Deep dive: Acute kidney injury and timing of renal replacement therapy
item.description:
A consultant-level review of renal replacement therapy (RRT) in ICU acute kidney injury. On timing: ELAIN (JAMA 2016, single centre, 231 patients) found lower 90-day mortality with early RRT. AKIKI (NEJM 2016, 620 patients), IDEAL-ICU (NEJM 2018, 488 patients with septic shock, stopped for futility) and STARRT-AKI (NEJM 2020, 3,019 randomised) found no mortality benefit. STARRT-AKI also found more adverse events with accelerated RRT and more RRT dependence at 90 days (10.4% vs 6.0%, RR 1.74). A 2025 post hoc analysis suggests this excess dependence comes mostly from starting RRT at all rather than starting it early. In the 2020 Lancet IPD meta-analysis, 28-day mortality was 44% vs 43%. Between about 38% and 49% of patients in the delayed arms never needed RRT. AKIKI2 (Lancet 2021) found no extra benefit from waiting beyond 72 hours of oliguria or a BUN of 112 mg/dL, and an adjusted secondary analysis showed a mortality signal (HR 1.65). BICARICU-2 (JAMA 2025) did not change mortality, though RRT use was lower with bicarbonate (a secondary outcome). On modality: Hemodiafe found no survival difference, and the excess dialysis dependence seen with intermittent RRT is an observational finding only. On dose: ATN and RENAL support delivering 20-25 mL/kg/h; LIMIT (12 vs 25 mL/kg/h) is ongoing. On anticoagulation: in RICH, citrate gave longer filter life and less bleeding than heparin, with no significant mortality difference and more new infections. On stopping: urine output without diuretics is the best predictor of success. LIBERATE-D (JAMA 2026, 221 stable patients on intermittent haemodialysis) found more recovery with a conservative dialysis strategy, but only in the unadjusted analysis. Long term, about 5% of RENAL day-90 survivors needed maintenance dialysis at four years, and albuminuria was common. On guidance: KDIGO 2012 is still current, and its 2026 AKI/AKD update completed public review in May 2026 and is awaiting publication. NICE NG148 (2019, updated 2024) and the 2020 joint Renal Association/BRS/ICS guideline both advise basing initiation on the whole patient.

Take-home points

  • Without an emergent indication, early RRT does not reduce mortality, and waiting means roughly a third to a half of patients never need it.
  • Don't wait indefinitely: AKIKI2 gives a signal of harm from delaying beyond 72 hours of oliguria or a urea of about 40 mmol/L when nothing else has prompted RRT.
  • Deliver 20 to 25 mL/kg/h, and use regional citrate for CRRT unless there is a contraindication.
  • Choose modality on haemodynamic stability and brain injury, not dogma.
  • Watch urine output, don't use diuretics to speed weaning, and arrange kidney follow-up for survivors.

item.title: Deep dive: Weaning, extubation and tracheostomy
item.description:
A consultant-level tour of liberation from ventilation. Short pressure-support breathing trials (Subira 2019) increase successful extubation without raising reintubation, though TIP-EX (2022) found no ventilator-free-day benefit in high-risk patients; 2024 meta-analyses favour pressure augmentation. After extubation, high-flow beats standard oxygen in low-risk patients, and in high-risk patients high-flow alternating with NIV (HIGH-WEAN) or humidified NIV in very high risk reduces reintubation; ATS/CHEST 2017 and ERS 2022 favour NIV for high risk. Prophylactic methylprednisolone works mainly in patients who fail a cuff leak test, a test with high specificity but modest sensitivity. TracMan showed no mortality benefit from tracheostomy within four days and showed how poorly clinicians predict prolonged ventilation; Cochrane 2015 hinted at benefit, and SETPOINT2 was neutral in stroke. Percutaneous and surgical techniques have similar serious complication rates, with fewer wound infections after percutaneous. UK safety work (NAP4, the NTSP 2020 guidance and the 20-hospital improvement programme) centres on care after insertion. Prolonged weaning (WIND) carries high mortality; diaphragm atrophy predicts prolonged ventilation; and RESCUE-3 phrenic stimulation (2026) is promising but stopped early, with more serious adverse events.

Take-home points

  • A short pressure support SBT is fine for most patients and doesn't increase reintubation.
  • High-risk patients go on to high-flow alternating with NIV after extubation; low-risk patients get high-flow.
  • Do a cuff leak test in high-risk patients; if it fails, give steroids at least four hours ahead, ideally twelve.
  • In TracMan, early tracheostomy didn't save lives: decide case by case and remember how badly we predict who will need one.
  • Use NTSP bedhead signs, emergency algorithms and capnography for every tracheostomy, every time.

item.title: Deep dive: Severe community-acquired pneumonia on ICU
item.description:
A consultant-level comparison of the 2023 ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT severe CAP guideline with the 2019 ATS/IDSA guideline, the 2025 ATS-only update (which IDSA declined to endorse) and NICE NG250 (September 2025, replacing NG138 and CG191; BTS remains 2009 with a 2015 annotated update). The European panel prefers a macrolide, not a fluoroquinolone, as the beta-lactam partner, based on observational data; ACCESS (2024) shows clarithromycin improves a surrogate early-response endpoint in ward patients, and a 2025 network meta-analysis finds no regimen convincingly superior. Guidelines converge on covering MRSA and Pseudomonas only when there are validated risk factors, using nasal MRSA PCR and cultures to de-escalate. Multiplex PCR speeds escalation but not de-escalation in the one large RCT. Steroids are covered briefly (CAPE COD positive, REMAP-CAP hydrocortisone stopped for futility; NICE 2025 now says consider a steroid). The main news is REMAP-CAP's influenza antiviral domain (preprint, 2026): in 442 critically ill patients, oseltamivir for 5 or 10 days was associated with higher 90-day mortality than no antiviral, which challenges every current guideline. Duration: 5 days per NICE, at least 5 per ATS 2025, with procalcitonin to shorten per ERS. BALANCE supports 7 rather than 14 days in bacteraemia.

Take-home points

  • Beta-lactam plus macrolide is the default in severe CAP; keep levofloxacin for true penicillin allergy and be careful combining it with steroids (MHRA).
  • Cover MRSA or Pseudomonas only with prior respiratory isolation or recent admission with IV antibiotics, and use nasal MRSA PCR and cultures to de-escalate quickly.
  • Rapid multiplex panels only help if someone acts on the result the same day: in the RCT they sped up escalation, not de-escalation.
  • Oseltamivir is no longer automatic in ventilated or shocked influenza after REMAP-CAP (preprint): discuss with microbiology and recruit to trials.
  • Five to seven days of antibiotics for most patients, guided by clinical stability and procalcitonin.

item.title: Deep dive: Non-invasive respiratory support and timing of intubation
item.description:
A consultant-level review of non-invasive support in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. FLORALI (NEJM 2015) found no difference in intubation between high-flow nasal oxygen, standard oxygen and face-mask NIV, but a secondary 90-day mortality signal favoured high flow. The larger SOHO trial (NEJM 2026, 1,110 patients) found identical 28-day mortality (14.6% in both arms) and only slightly less intubation with high flow (42.4% vs 48.4%). Helmet NIV looked dramatic in a small single-centre trial stopped early (Patel, JAMA 2016). HENIVOT (COVID, JAMA 2021) missed its primary outcome but intubated fewer patients, and HELMET-COVID found no mortality difference. In RECOVERY-RS (JAMA 2022), CPAP reduced intubation or death compared with conventional oxygen (36.3% vs 44.4%) and high flow did not. RENOVATE (JAMA 2025) found high flow non-inferior to NIV in four of five groups. Guidelines: ERS/ATS 2017 made no recommendation on NIV for de novo hypoxaemic failure. ERS 2022 conditionally prefers high flow over NIV. ESICM 2023 strongly recommends high flow over conventional oxygen to reduce intubation, but makes no recommendation on NIV or CPAP versus high flow, or on helmet versus mask. The new ATS 2026 guideline gives a strong recommendation for high flow and a conditional one for NIV or CPAP. The BTS high-flow clinical statement is still pending. Patient self-inflicted lung injury rests on physiological and animal data and is contested. ROX (Roca 2019) and HACOR (Duan 2017) predict failure with modest-to-good accuracy. Evidence that delayed intubation causes harm is observational and confounded, the target trial emulations conflict, and there is no randomised trial of timing.

Take-home points

  • Compared with standard oxygen, high flow reduces intubation, but SOHO (NEJM 2026) shows no mortality benefit.
  • CPAP or helmet NIV are reasonable escalation steps, but guideline support is only conditional and the trial data are mostly from COVID.
  • P-SILI is plausible but unproven: use it as a reason to watch inspiratory effort, not as a reason to intubate.
  • ROX and HACOR help, but follow the trend and set a time to reassess (one to two hours) with named criteria.
  • Harm from delayed intubation isn't proven, but patients who fail do badly: decide early and document the plan and ceiling of treatment.

item.title: Deep dive: Pulmonary embolism with right ventricular failure
item.description:
A consultant-level look at intermediate-high and high-risk pulmonary embolism. PEITHO (NEJM 2014, 1,005 patients) found that full-dose tenecteplase cut death or haemodynamic decompensation at 7 days from 5.6% to 2.6%. It raised extracranial bleeding (6.3% vs 1.2%) and stroke (2.4% vs 0.2%), with no mortality benefit at 30 days or at about 3 years. ESC 2019 therefore reserved systemic lysis for high-risk PE and for rescue. Reduced-dose lysis is common in UK practice (ERUPT audit), but the outcome trial, PEITHO-3, has not yet reported. HI-PEITHO (NEJM 2026, 544 patients) is the first RCT in which a catheter therapy beat anticoagulation alone on a clinical composite: 4.0% vs 10.3% at 7 days, RR 0.39, with no intracranial haemorrhage. The benefit was driven by decompensation, though, and 14 of the 28 control-arm events met only the NEWS of 9 or more criterion. The trial was open-label and industry-funded, and 30-day deaths were 6 vs 3. PEERLESS, STORM-PE and CANARY measured mostly process or surrogate outcomes. The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline introduced categories A to E. It makes systemic lysis, catheter therapy and surgery all reasonable in category E1 and possible in category D, and gives PERT a class 1 recommendation, but its evidence review predates HI-PEITHO. NICE NG158 still says not to lyse stable patients. Supportive care means cautious fluid, early noradrenaline, high-flow oxygen and treating intubation as peri-arrest. VA-ECMO is a bridge, with observational pooled mortality of about 43%. UK surgical embolectomy is rare and carries about 25% in-hospital mortality.

Take-home points

  • Full-dose systemic lysis prevents collapse in intermediate-risk PE but increases bleeding and haemorrhagic stroke and doesn't reduce mortality: keep it for shock or deterioration.
  • HI-PEITHO supports catheter-directed lysis for intermediate-high-risk patients with tachycardia, tachypnoea or borderline blood pressure, but the benefit is fewer decompensations (half of control-arm events were a NEWS of 9 or more alone), not fewer deaths.
  • For the failing RV, be cautious with fluid, start noradrenaline early, prefer high-flow oxygen and treat intubation as a peri-arrest procedure.
  • Know your local pathway (PERT, catheter therapy, surgery and VA-ECMO) and how to reach it out of hours.
  • Watch for PEITHO-3 (reduced-dose alteplase), PEERLESS II and PERSEVERE (thrombectomy in high-risk PE).

item.title: Deep dive: Corticosteroids in septic shock and severe pneumonia
item.description:
In septic shock, ADRENAL (3,800 ventilated patients, hydrocortisone infusion) showed faster shock resolution but no 90-day mortality benefit, while APROCCHSS (1,241 sicker patients, hydrocortisone boluses plus enteral fludrocortisone) cut 90-day mortality from 49% to 43%. The 2023 individual-patient meta-analysis found no overall mortality effect, with a signal only for regimens that included fludrocortisone. Observational target-trial emulation supports adding fludrocortisone, but a 2024 phase II dose-finding trial did not, and RECORDS is still recruiting. In severe community-acquired pneumonia, CAPE COD (hydrocortisone, which excluded shock and influenza) halved 28-day mortality. REMAP-CAP's open-label 7-day hydrocortisone arm stopped for futility with a numerically worse result, and its population, allocation and control-arm contamination all differ from CAPE COD. ESCAPe (methylprednisolone) was neutral. On who benefits: in a 2025 individual-patient meta-analysis the benefit was confined to patients with CRP above 204 mg/L. Post hoc transcriptomic (SRS2, consensus subtype CTS2) and biomarker (CAPE COD reanalysis) work suggests immune-profile-dependent benefit or harm, but none of it is ready for the bedside. On guidelines: SSC 2026 gives a conditional suggestion for steroids in septic shock. SCCM 2024 is conditional for shock and strong for severe CAP. ERS/ESICM 2023 supports steroids in severe CAP only with shock and predates CAPE COD. ATS 2025 (without IDSA) reverses the 2019 ATS/IDSA advice with a conditional yes for severe CAP. NICE NG250 (2025) says consider them for high-severity CAP, IV hydrocortisone first, for 4 to 7 days.

Take-home points

  • In septic shock, hydrocortisone reliably shortens shock; any survival benefit is small and may depend on adding fludrocortisone.
  • In severe CAP without shock or influenza, CAPE COD supports early hydrocortisone, and NICE (2025) and the ATS (2025) now agree.
  • REMAP-CAP means you shouldn't assume the CAPE COD benefit carries over to patients with shock or to later starts.
  • High CRP is the best bedside hint of who benefits; biomarker and gene-expression subtypes aren't ready for clinical use.
  • Watch glucose and sodium, and document why you started.

item.title: Deep dive: Red cell transfusion thresholds in critical illness
item.description:
A restrictive threshold of 70 g/L remains right for most critically ill adults, including septic shock (TRISS; ESICM 2020; NICE NG24; Cochrane 2025, 61 trials, no overall mortality difference). The exceptions are now clearer. In acute MI, MINT (2023) and a 2025 patient-level meta-analysis lean towards harm from restrictive transfusion, especially in type 1 MI, and the 2025 AABB AMI guideline suggests a liberal trigger of 100 g/L. NICE NG24 still says 80 g/L with a target of 80 to 100 g/L in ACS: the 2026 update covered tranexamic acid only. In acute brain injury, TRAIN and the 2025 Cochrane update favour about 90 g/L. After cardiac surgery, TRICS III supports 75 g/L, and older patients did better with restrictive transfusion in a subgroup. TITRe2 showed a secondary mortality signal. In haematological malignancy the evidence is very low certainty, with a single-centre cancer septic shock trial (TRICOP) signalling benefit from liberal transfusion at 90 days. The frail elderly answer awaits LIBERAL (completed, unpublished) and, for younger cardiac surgical patients, TRICS IV.

Take-home points

  • Seventy grams per litre is still right for most of the ICU, including septic shock: TRISS holds.
  • Acute MI is the big exception. MINT, the 2025 patient-level meta-analysis and the 2025 AABB guideline lean to 100 g/L, while NICE NG24's 80 g/L hasn't been revisited.
  • In acute brain injury the evidence favours a trigger of around 90 g/L, as the 2025 Cochrane update now shows.
  • Use 75 g/L after cardiac surgery, and don't assume older patients need more blood (TRICS III age subgroup, FOCUS).
  • Watch for LIBERAL (older non-cardiac surgical patients) and TRICS IV (patients 65 and under having cardiac surgery).

item.title: Deep dive: Fluids in sepsis
item.description:
A consultant-level look at sepsis fluid resuscitation. FEAST (2011) showed boluses can harm, and three adult trials of restrictive versus liberal fluid found no mortality difference: CLASSIC (2022, ICU septic shock), CLOVERS (2023, emergency department hypotension, stopped for futility) and ARISE FLUIDS (NEJM 2026, early vasopressors). ARISE FLUIDS did show less pulmonary oedema with the restrictive approach. Each of these trials enrolled patients who had already received fluid. For fluid choice, SMART was positive while BaSICS and PLUS were neutral. The Hammond 2022 and BEST-Living 2024 meta-analyses put the probability that balanced crystalloids reduce mortality at about 90 percent, with a harm signal in traumatic brain injury. ALBIOS, the German ARISS trial (stopped early) and the UK ABC-Sepsis feasibility trial found no survival benefit from albumin, and ALCAMIST is still recruiting. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 found that a personalised protocol targeting capillary refill time beat usual care on a hierarchical outcome, mainly through shorter organ support. The guidelines differ. Surviving Sepsis 2026 still suggests at least 30 mL/kg in the first 3 hours (conditional, low certainty). ESICM 2025 suggests up to 30 mL/kg. NICE NG253 (November 2025) recommends 250 mL boluses up to 1 litre, then senior advice. The evidence for de-resuscitation is thin: the first version of GODIF stopped after 41 patients, and the main trial is ongoing.

Take-home points

  • The 30 mL/kg figure rests on low-certainty evidence. Surviving Sepsis 2026 says 'at least', ESICM 2025 says 'up to', and NICE NG253 says 250 mL boluses to 1 litre, then senior review. Reassess after every bolus.
  • Use balanced crystalloid by default (about 90 percent probability of a small mortality benefit), but use saline in traumatic brain injury.
  • After initial resuscitation, restrictive and liberal strategies have the same mortality (CLASSIC, CLOVERS, ARISE FLUIDS). Early noradrenaline, given peripherally if needed, is reasonable and led to less pulmonary oedema in ARISE FLUIDS.
  • Guide further fluid with capillary refill time and dynamic responsiveness tests such as passive leg raise or stroke volume response, not static CVP alone (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2, ESICM 2025).
  • Albumin is not first line (ALBIOS, ARISS, ABC-Sepsis). Consider de-resuscitation once the patient is stable, but the trial evidence is thin and GODIF is still running.

item.title: Deep dive: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage on ICU
item.description:
A consultant-level tour of ICU management after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Oral nimodipine (British Aneurysm Nimodipine Trial, 1989) is still the only drug proven to improve outcome. Magnesium (MASH-2), simvastatin (STASH), ultra-early tranexamic acid (ULTRA) and clazosentan (CONSCIOUS-3 and REACT) were all neutral for functional outcome, even when clazosentan reduced vasospasm. The rescue therapies for delayed cerebral ischaemia rest on thin evidence. Induced hypertension has one underpowered trial (HIMALAIA, 41 patients). Endovascular rescue has one small phase 2 trial (IMCVS) with worse 6-month mRS. EARLYDRAIN (JAMA Neurology 2023) cut unfavourable outcome from 44.8% to 32.6%, but the 2026 ESO/EANS/ESMINT guideline pooled it and made no recommendation. The guidelines diverge most on TCD: NICE NG228 advises against it outside research, while AHA/ASA 2023 rates it reasonable. SAHaRA (NEJM 2025) found no benefit from liberal transfusion. Population case fatality has stayed at about a third for two decades. Observational data on withdrawal of treatment and on early invasive care for grade V patients point to a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Take-home points

  • Give oral nimodipine to everyone. If it drops the pressure, manage the hypotension (for example with a vasopressor) rather than stopping it, and only pause it if blood pressure swings are significant.
  • Aim for euvolaemia, not hypervolaemia. Treat natriuretic hyponatraemia (fludrocortisone or hydrocortisone is reasonable per AHA) and don't fluid restrict.
  • Magnesium, statins, clazosentan and pre-treatment tranexamic acid don't improve outcome. Treating vasospasm is not the same as treating the patient.
  • Induced hypertension, intra-arterial therapy/angioplasty and prophylactic lumbar drainage are reasonable but unproven. NICE, AHA/ASA and ESO differ on them, and on TCD.
  • Don't withdraw treatment early on admission grade alone. Treat hydrocephalus and reassess, because clinical improvement before aneurysm treatment strongly predicts a good outcome.

item.title: Deep dive: Severe traumatic brain injury on ICU
item.description:
A consultant-level look at severe TBI on ICU. BEST-TRIP (NEJM 2012) compared two treatment protocols rather than ICP monitoring versus none, and found no difference. DECRA (NEJM 2011) found early bifrontal craniectomy worse at 6 months, no longer significant at 12. RESCUEicp (NEJM 2016) found that last-tier craniectomy cut mortality (about 27 vs 49 percent at 6 months), but many of the extra survivors were vegetative or dependent at 24 months. OXY-TC (Lancet Neurol 2023) found no benefit from adding brain tissue oxygen to ICP-guided care. BOOST-3 has not reported; it is active, not recruiting, with primary completion estimated for November 2027. On transfusion, HEMOTION (NEJM 2024; threshold 10 vs 7 g/dL) was non-significant but favoured liberal, and TRAIN (JAMA 2024; 9 vs 7 g/dL, mixed acute brain injury) was positive. TRAIN's TBI-only secondary analysis (JAMA Netw Open, Sept 2026) had a fragility index of 1, and meta-analyses disagree. CRASH-3 (Lancet 2019) showed no benefit from tranexamic acid in severe TBI, yet NICE NG232 (2023) says to consider it for GCS 12 or less within 2 hours. BTF 4th edition (2016; ICP above 22, CPP 60-70) contrasts with the SIBICC consensus tiered algorithms (2019/2020). IMPACT and CRASH models predict outcomes for populations. Cohort data on withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment (Canadian 2011, CENTER-TBI 2021) and late recovery (TRACK-TBI 2021) show the risk of a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Take-home points

  • BEST-TRIP tested protocols, not the monitor: use ICP and escalate in tiers (SIBICC is expert consensus, not trial evidence).
  • Last-tier craniectomy (RESCUEicp) saves lives, but many extra survivors are vegetative or dependent; discuss this with families before surgery. Early bifrontal craniectomy for diffuse injury (DECRA) did not help.
  • Brain tissue oxygen-guided care is unproven: OXY-TC was neutral and BOOST-3 has not yet reported.
  • Lean towards a liberal transfusion threshold (around 9 g/dL), but the TBI-specific evidence is fragile (HEMOTION non-significant; TRAIN TBI fragility index 1).
  • Be cautious about early withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment: much TBI mortality follows withdrawal, practice varies widely between centres, and some patients recover late.

item.title: Deep dive: Temperature control after cardiac arrest
item.description:
Deep dive from the 2002 HACA and Bernard hypothermia trials through TTM (33 vs 36 degrees, 2013), HYPERION (non-shockable, 2019), TTM2 (2021, hypothermia vs actively fever-controlled normothermia, no difference in 6-month death, more arrhythmia with cooling), HACA-IHCA (underpowered, futile), the BOX duration trial (36 vs 72 h fever prevention) and ICECAP (JAMA 2026, longer cooling does not help, no normothermia arm). Covers the 2025 ERC-ESICM shift from targeted temperature management to temperature control with fever prevention (at or below 37.5 C for 36 to 72 h, feedback device, no cold-fluid prehospital cooling, no active rewarming of mild hypothermia), differences with the AHA, practical management, outcomes, and grey zones: shockable and non-shockable subgroups, in-hospital arrest, illness severity, and ongoing trials STEPCARE (TEMP-CARE), IH-TTM and R-CAST OHCA.

Take-home points

  • The question has changed from 'cool to 33' to 'have I prevented fever': target 37.5 C or below with continuous core temperature monitoring.
  • ERC-ESICM 2025 suggests preventing fever for 36 to 72 hours; the BOX trial found no difference between 36 and 72 hours of device-based fever prevention.
  • If a device is used, use one with feedback; whether devices beat simple measures is being tested in STEPCARE (TEMP-CARE).
  • Do not actively rewarm comatose patients who arrive mildly hypothermic (32-36 C), and do not use routine prehospital cold-fluid cooling.
  • Hypothermia is not proven dead in non-shockable, in-hospital or illness-severity subgroups, but there is no good evidence to chase it outside a trial.

item.title: Deep dive: Prolonged disorders of consciousness: diagnosis and assessment
item.description:
A consultant-level review of PDOC diagnosis. Clinical consensus misclassifies roughly four in ten patients labelled vegetative as minimally conscious (Schnakers 2009), and a single C R S R misdiagnoses about a third (Wannez 2017), so repeated structured assessment is the standard. Task-based f M R I and E E G studies (Monti 2010, Claassen 2019, Bodien 2024) show covert command following in a minority of behaviourally unresponsive patients (25 percent of 241 in Bodien), but these are research tools with a high false-negative rate. The A A N 2018 and E A N 2020 guidelines are more open to such tools than the R C P 2020 guideline, which restricts them to registered research. The episode covers the R C P pathway (specialist referral beyond 4 weeks, at least ten C R S R occasions over 2 to 3 weeks, re-evaluation at 6 and 12 months), amantadine in traumatic PDOC, prognosis by aetiology and the R C P chronic and permanent definitions, and briefly the Mental Capacity Act angle.

Take-home points

  • Do not rely on a single bedside look: use the C R S R repeatedly (R C P: at least ten occasions over two to three weeks) after excluding sedatives, seizures, hydrocephalus and metabolic causes.
  • Anyone still disordered beyond four weeks should be referred to a specialist PDOC unit; consider amantadine for traumatic cases at 4 to 16 weeks (A A N Level B).
  • Covert awareness is real (cognitive motor dissociation in 25 percent of non-responders in Bodien 2024) but f M R I and E E G paradigms are research tools; a negative result does not exclude awareness.
  • The R C P 2020 guideline and the E A N 2020 guideline give opposite advice on activation paradigms; know your local position and document practicable steps under the Mental Capacity Act.
  • Prognosis favours traumatic over non-traumatic aetiology and M C S over vegetative state; trajectory on serial C R S R matters more than the label.

item.title: Deep dive: Death by neurological criteria (brainstem death testing)
item.description:
The Academy of Medical Royal Colleges 2025 Code of Practice (in use from 1 January 2025) replaced the 2008 Code without changing the definition of death. Key changes: apnoea test start PaCO2 at least 5.3 kPa, minimum 5 minutes, end PaCO2 at least 8.0 kPa, rise at least 2.7 kPa, pH below 7.3; time of death is now the completion of the second set of clinical tests (or the point the final two doctors are satisfied if ancillary investigation follows) rather than the first set; core temperature at least 36 C; sodium 125 to 160 mmol/L; red-flag groups folded into preconditions; ancillary investigation required when full examination or apnoea test is impossible or confounders cannot be excluded (including decompressive craniectomy and therapeutic steroids); CT angiography is the UK consensus ancillary test of choice, whereas the 2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM guideline recommends against it and a 2025 Canadian prospective study found CTA and CT perfusion did not reach a 98 percent accuracy threshold. ECMO requirements are unchanged, with supplementary 2020 UK guidance awaiting update. UK (brainstem) and US (whole brain) formulations differ conceptually but the bedside examination is near identical; the WBDP 2020 and AAN 2023 documents are consensus, not trial evidence. Case law (Bland, Re M 2020, Dance 2022, Casey 2023, DT 2025 EWCOP, Barts v MC 2025) holds that a person is not dead in law until Code-compliant testing, that disputes about testing go to the Court of Protection on best interests, and that once death is properly established there is no best interests analysis. NHSBT reports neurological testing in potential donors fell to 63 percent in March 2025 from 72 percent the year before, with DCD now 62 percent of deceased donors.

Take-home points

  • Know the 2025 Code numbers: apnoea start PaCO2 at least 5.3 kPa, 5 minutes minimum, end at least 8.0 kPa with rise at least 2.7 kPa and pH below 7.3; core temperature at least 36 C; time of death is at completion of the second set.
  • Ancillary investigation is required in defined circumstances (incomplete examination or apnoea test, confounders such as residual sedation, craniectomy, therapeutic steroids); document why, and do not treat CT angiography as infallible given the UK consensus versus US guideline and Canadian data.
  • On ECMO the criteria are unchanged; plan sweep or CO2 titration for the apnoea test and sample sites (on VA-ECMO, left and right distal arterial gases) with supplementary guidance.
  • If a family objects to testing or the diagnosis, follow Code 6.69: talk early, offer the lay summary and observation of tests, seek legal advice within days. Until Code-compliant testing the person is not dead in law; disputes about testing in adults go to the Court of Protection on best interests.
  • Test promptly: neurological testing in potential donors fell to 63 percent in March 2025 and the CMOs wrote in February 2026 backing the Code.

item.title: Deep dive: Withdrawing CANH in prolonged disorders of consciousness after Re Y
item.description:
In An NHS Trust v Y (2018) the Supreme Court held that withdrawing clinically assisted nutrition and hydration from a patient with a prolonged disorder of consciousness does not need a court order where the Mental Capacity Act and professional guidance are followed and there is agreement. Kate and Tom go through who the decision-maker is, the process in the BMA/RCP 2018 CANH guidance and the RCP 2020 PDOC guidelines, what the independent second opinion must involve, and when a case is finely balanced or disputed enough that it must go to the Court of Protection (including the 2020 Vice President's guidance). They look at how later judgments have applied this: criticism of years of drift in GU, AB and XR, a case where the court ordered CANH to continue against medical advice (YD, 2025), and a 2026 Mid Yorkshire case. They finish with what it means for early decisions on ICU.

Take-home points

  • Re Y removed the mandatory court application, not the scrutiny: with the MCA followed, the guidance observed and agreement reached, no court order is needed.
  • A finely balanced decision, a difference of medical opinion or a lack of agreement means a prompt Court of Protection application.
  • The safeguard the Supreme Court relied on is a genuinely independent second opinion with its own examination.
  • Drift is the failure the courts keep criticising: continuing CANH by default is not neutral, and the giving has to be justified.
  • Start and document the values conversation on ICU; it becomes core evidence later.

item.title: Deep dive: ARDS phenotypes and personalised ventilation
item.description:
Kate and Tom ask whether ARDS can yet be treated as more than one disease. Secondary analyses of older trials found hyper- and hypo-inflammatory subphenotypes that differ in prognosis and may respond differently to fluids, PEEP and simvastatin. The prospective UK PHIND study shows they can be identified near the bedside within about an hour, and the UK PANTHER platform trial is now testing phenotype-guided treatment (no results yet). They also cover the 2024 global definition (a consensus statement), driving pressure and mechanical power as associations rather than proven targets, harm or no benefit from personalised PEEP strategies (ART, EPVent-2, LIVE, EITVent), proning (PROSEVA), the ACURASYS versus ROSE paralysis story, DEXA-ARDS and steroids, and EOLIA and ECMO, then where the ESICM 2023, ATS 2024 and FICM/ICS guidelines diverge.

Take-home points

  • Inflammatory subphenotypes are reproducible and prognostic, but treating by phenotype belongs in trials until PANTHER-type trials report.
  • Driving pressure and mechanical power are associations from observational and mediation analyses, not proven targets: use them as warning lights.
  • Avoid prolonged high-pressure recruitment (ART showed harm), and prone early and for 16 hours or more when P/F is below 150 mmHg.
  • Routine paralysis is where guidelines split most (ESICM against, ATS conditionally for early severe ARDS): use it selectively.
  • Talk to an ECMO centre early for EOLIA-type patients. Steroids are suggested by ATS 2024 but not addressed by ESICM 2023 or FICM/ICS.

item.title: Deep dive: Vasopressors in septic shock
item.description:
Consultant-level look at vasopressor decisions in septic shock, built around the 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines. Early noradrenaline (CENSER, CLOVERS) looks safe but has not been shown to reduce mortality. Observational data and the 2026 guideline support starting peripherally rather than waiting for a central line. VASST and the UK VANISH trial place vasopressin as a catecholamine-sparing add-on rather than a life-saver, and observational data link later vasopressin starts with higher mortality. ATHOS-3 and a small single-centre methylene blue trial show blood pressure gains without proven survival benefit. On MAP targets, SEPSISPAM, the UK 65 trial and Japan's OPTPRESS (stopped early for harm with the higher target) underpin the new suggestion of 60 to 65 mmHg in patients aged 65 or over. Terlipressin and selepressin don't help.

Take-home points

  • Early noradrenaline is safe but has not been shown to save lives.
  • Start vasopressors peripherally rather than delay for a central line.
  • Target a MAP of 65 mmHg, or 60 to 65 in patients aged 65 or over; higher targets have looked harmful.
  • Add vasopressin as the noradrenaline dose rises: it spares catecholamine but has not shown a survival benefit.
  • Angiotensin II and methylene blue are rescue options with weak evidence; avoid terlipressin.

item.title: Deep dive: Acute myocardial infarction in the ICU
item.description:
Kate and Tom cover what reaches the ICU after myocardial infarction: culprit-only PCI in cardiogenic shock (CULPRIT-SHOCK), the negative ECLS-SHOCK trial of early VA-ECMO, the positive but complication-heavy DanGer Shock trial of the microaxial pump, immediate versus delayed angiography after cardiac arrest (COACT, TOMAHAWK), type 2 MI and troponin interpretation, and perioperative myocardial injury (VISION, MANAGE).

Take-home points

  • Culprit-only PCI in infarct-related shock; no routine intra-aortic balloon pump.
  • Routine early VA-ECMO did not improve 30-day survival in ECLS-SHOCK and roughly doubled bleeding and vascular complications.
  • In DanGer Shock a microaxial pump improved survival in selected STEMI shock patients (not comatose after arrest) at the cost of more complications; involve the shock team early.
  • After arrest, ST elevation goes to the cath lab; stable patients without it can have delayed angiography.
  • Do not treat a type 2 troponin rise like a type 1 infarction: treat the cause.

item.title: Deep dive: Neuroprognostication after cardiac arrest
item.description:
Kate and Tom walk through the 2025 ERC-ESICM prognostication algorithm for comatose survivors of cardiac arrest: the wider entry point (motor score below 6 at 72 hours or later), the two-or-more rule for poor outcome, the new favourable indicators, why neurofilament light is not yet recommended, bias from self-fulfilling prophecy and early withdrawal, and the UK best-interests framework (MCA 2005, Aintree v James, Re Y, RCP PDOC guidance).

Take-home points

  • Wait until at least 72 hours, exclude confounders (sedation, relaxants, temperature, hypotension, sepsis, metabolic) and examine carefully.
  • Poor outcome is likely only with two or more concordant predictors; one alone is not enough.
  • Look for favourable signs too (motor score 4 or 5, normal NSE, continuous EEG, no MRI diffusion restriction); indeterminate means observe and reassess, because late awakening happens.
  • NSE needs serial samples (24, 48, 72 h) and care over haemolysis; the guideline does not recommend neurofilament light yet.
  • Prognosis informs a best-interests decision but does not make it; keep the prognosis and withdrawal conversations separate and document.

item.title: 7 October 2026 (extended): PRESSURE, neuroprognosis in the Court of Protection, and an ICU-referral PFD
item.description:
Covers 30 September to 7 October 2026. Extended edition (about 45 minutes); replaces the earlier versions from today. Items first published before 30 September are marked as recent context.

  • MHRA: no new National Patient Safety Alerts, device safety notices or Drug Safety Update this week. The field safety notice list for 28 Sep to 2 Oct was not yet published. There was a minor leaflet defect for levetiracetam granules (EL(26)A/40). MHRA alerts
  • PRESSURE (JAMA, 28 Sep; recent context). 1,900 ventilated children in 23 paediatric ICUs: a permissive MAP target above the 5th centile meant 37.5% less vasoactive drug for a 3 mmHg difference in pressure. Primary outcome: probabilistic index 0.52 (0.49 to 0.54). Takeaway: less is not proven better, but more is not obviously better. Paper · ICCN commentary
  • SAFER (AJRCCM, 30 Sep). Pulse vs non-pulse methylprednisolone in acute exacerbation of IPF, n=100: no significant mortality difference, with very wide confidence intervals. Paper · PulmCrit on pulse steroids
  • A2B secondary analysis (Anaesthesia, 6 Oct). Patient-reported ICU experience was no better with alpha-2 agonist sedation than with propofol; only 29% of survivors responded. Paper
  • BJA editorial on the AGP list (2 Oct). Scotland has dropped its aerosol-generating procedure list and moved to risk-based "air transmission" categories. England still has the list. The authors sat on the guidance panels. Editorial
  • Videolaryngoscopy, VCISpain (Anaesthesia, 2 Oct). 5,302 intubations: even with an excellent view, about 6% of first attempts were difficult or failed. Document the blade, the view and how the tube was delivered. Paper
  • SGLT2 inhibitors before surgery. The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline reaffirms its 2024 advice to stop 3 to 4 days before. UK CPOC/JBDS guidance: omit them the day before and the day of surgery, longer with bowel prep, and check ketones. CPOC/JBDS
  • A Hospital Trust v MB [2026] EWCOP 32 (newly available). Withdrawal of ventilation after cardiac arrest. The evidence was framed on ERC/ESICM 2025 multimodal criteria, and the judgment explains why SSEP was not done. Judgment
  • Cardiff and Vale UHB v ST [2026] EWCOP 44 (30 Sep). NG feeding withdrawn despite the family's faith-based objection. Repeated tube removal was treated as evidence of her wishes. Judgment
  • Royal Berkshire NHS FT v BM [2026] EWCOP 50 (released 6 Oct). Surgery under GA was approved with a stepwise, last-resort restraint plan. Judgment
  • Prevention of Future Deaths reports. Ref 2026-0390 (South Wales Central, 30 Sep): ED overcrowding, and prescribed antibiotics never given. Ref 2026-0353 (Essex, 17 Sep; recent context): a dispute over ICU admission criteria delayed transfer. PFD reports
  • Townsend v Epsom and St Helier. The Supreme Court hearing is confirmed for 12 to 13 January 2027. UKSC
  • PARAMEDIC-3 Bayesian analysis (Resuscitation, 25 Sep; recent context). Intraosseous-first had about an 82% probability of worse 30-day survival, but any effect is probably modest; there was a 98% probability of worse ROSC. Stick with IV-first and IO as the fallback. Paper
  • Early PaO2 in acute brain injury (Neurocrit Care, 28 Sep; recent context). Lowest mortality at roughly 11-30 kPa (ICH), 13-25 kPa (SAH) and 13-21 kPa (ischaemic stroke); above about 40 kPa looks harmful. Observational. Paper
  • Brain-TTM (JCBFM, 2 Oct). In 34 patients, targeting brain temperature was no better than targeting systemic temperature; the brain ran about 0.3°C warmer during maintenance. Paper
  • Intra-operative hypotension and pneumonia (Anaesthesia, 2 Oct). Retrospective, 151,036 patients: relative falls from baseline predicted pneumonia better than absolute MAP thresholds, but the effect was small. Paper
  • Antibiotic timing by NEWS2 and shock (Lancet Respir Med; epub Aug, now in print). About 100,000 encounters: each hour of delay was associated with higher mortality with shock or NEWS2 of 7 or more, and not below 7. This supports the NEWS2-7 one-hour rule. Paper
